title: India's Factories Are Running Faster Than They Have in Three Months. The Cost of Running Them Is the Highest in Four Years.
excerpt: The HSBC India Manufacturing PMI rose to 55.0 in May on strong domestic demand. But input costs driven by the Middle East war are squeezing margins, and companies are stockpiling materials in case things get worse.
body:
India's manufacturing sector expanded at its fastest pace in three months in May, but the headline number masks a deeper anxiety: the cost of making things in India is now the highest it has been in nearly four years, and manufacturers are hoarding raw materials because they expect the situation to deteriorate further.

The HSBC India Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index, compiled by S&P Global, rose to 55.0 in May from 54.7 in April, beating the preliminary flash estimate of 54.3. Any reading above 50 indicates expansion, and 55.0 represents a solid performance — the best since February.

## The Demand Story Is Strong

New orders grew at their fastest rate since February, driven by civil engineering projects, competitive pricing, and what the survey called "favourable demand conditions." Factory output rose at its quickest pace in three months, with intermediate and capital goods leading the expansion.

Domestic demand was the primary engine. Export orders continued to grow but at their slowest pace in three months, reflecting the drag from global uncertainty — tariff threats from the United States, supply chain disruptions from the Middle East war, and weakening demand in key European markets.

Hiring continued, though the pace of job creation slowed from April. In a country that needs to generate millions of new formal jobs each year, even steady-state hiring in the manufacturing sector counts as good news.

## The Cost Crisis Is Real

This is where the numbers turn uncomfortable. Input price inflation in May was the second-strongest reading in roughly four years, excluding April's spike. The culprits are straightforward: energy, fuel, raw materials, and transportation — all inflated by the ongoing war in West Asia and the partial blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Capital goods producers faced the sharpest cost increases among the three sub-sectors tracked by the survey. But here is the squeeze: selling price inflation actually eased from April and remained below the rate of input cost growth. Companies are absorbing the pain rather than passing it on to customers, constrained by competitive pressures in a market where demand is strong but price-sensitive.

"Input cost inflation eased slightly on the month, and output price inflation slowed more sharply, suggesting a potential squeeze on manufacturers' margins," said Pranjul Bhandari, Chief India Economist at HSBC.

## The Stockpiling Signal

Perhaps the most revealing data point: manufacturers sharply increased purchasing activity in May — at the fastest rate in three months — partly to build contingency stocks. Companies are buying more raw materials not because they need them immediately, but because they fear prices will rise further or supplies will be disrupted.

This is precautionary behaviour, the industrial equivalent of filling your pantry before a storm. It suggests that even though the headline PMI looks healthy, the business community is bracing for worse.

Business confidence fell to its lowest level since February, though it remained in positive territory. Companies expressed hope that cost pressures would eventually ease, supported by strong order pipelines.

## What It Means for Markets and the RBI

The PMI data lands days before two critical events: the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy decision on Friday, June 5, and the release of January-March GDP data the same day.

The RBI is widely expected to hold the repo rate at 5.25%, but the debate about whether a rate hike is coming has intensified. Oil prices near $93 per barrel, a rupee at ₹95 to the dollar, and imported inflation from the Hormuz disruption are all pulling toward tighter policy. But hiking rates would hit the very manufacturers whose margins are already being squeezed.

For NRI investors tracking India's growth story, the PMI offers a mixed signal: the factory floor is busy, but the war in West Asia is eroding the profitability that makes India's manufacturing boom sustainable.

**Sources:** S&P Global, HSBC, Reuters, Mint, Hindu Business Line
author: Diaspora Desk
